newsitem.title: POLAND: IPOs, polls seen capping Polish bourse rise in 97.
newsitem.headline: IPOs, polls seen capping Polish bourse rise in 97.

text.p: After surging 80 percent this year the Warsaw bourse looks fairly valued, analysts said, but they still see some upside potential despite long-awaited large initial public offerings and a parliamentary election.
Analysts said another factor, the central bank's threat to raise interest rates if rapid credit growth continues, could cool market sentiment as soon as the first quarter.

"What you've had in Poland in the last 18 months is an amazingly beneficial macroeconomic environment, and now for the first time there are a few blots appearing on the horizon," said Martin Taylor, Senior Investment Manager at Baring Assest Management in London.
Analysts said such blots were fast consumer spending, a widening current account deficit and stubborn inflation, all of which reflected an economy that needed slowing down.
BOURSE SEEN BEATING INFLATION NEXT YEAR

Taylor said the main WIG index, currently at 14,051.0 points, could reach 15,000 points in January before a rate rise helped send it as low as 12,000 points. It could however pick up in the fourth quarter after the elections.
Geoffrey Skipper, chief strategist at Poland's Korona mutual fund, said the bourse would likely end 1997 better than the 13-percent inflation the government forecasts.

Analysts said the main market, currently trading at 14 times earnings after rising about 60 percent this year in dollar terms, seemed fairly valued and might not draw foreign investment funds to the same degree as last year.
Others said the money could still flow.

"As we go down the curve from hedge funds to life funds, they're not going to be looking for high risk investments, which is a good sign for Poland because Poland is increasingly seen as one of the quality areas of emerging Europe," said Stephen Pettyfer, an analyst at Merrill Lynch in London.
Analysts also said the country's overall economic situation was good, with economic growth seen staying between five and six percent each year this decade.
LARGE IPOS COULD HURT LISTED STOCKS IN SHORT TERM
But they said a factor likely to hamper share-price rises at mid-year was the expected batch of large initial public offerings drawing capital from listed shares.

Last month Deputy Treasury Minister Wieslaw Kaczmarek warned of a glut next year if sales of large firms such as telecom monopolist Telekomunikacja Polska SA, insurer PZU SA and metals trader Impexmetal SA were not deftly alligned.

But analysts say such privatisations may continue to be delayed, especially in an election year, and that as few as one or two may actually take place in 1997, most likely those of copper concern KGKM Polska Miedz SA and Bank Handlowy SA.
The latter two would each add $1-$2 billion to the market capitalisation currently around $8 billion.
Some analysts said the Handlowy IPO could draw money from listed banks, which make up about 40 percent of market cap, but others said investors might buy listed stocks as well.

"I'm not sure about this outflow from listed to new firms because if you've got Bank Rozwoju Eksportu -- a solid bank -- or Wielkopolski Bank Kredytowy SA, I don't suppose I would just dump them and buy Bank Handlowy or PBK (Powszechny Bank Kredytowy SA)," said Jacek Dzierwa, Polish Equity Analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.
IPOS SEEN ATTRACTING CAPITAL IN LONGER TERM

Whatever their immediate effect, analysts said the listing of more large-cap industrials would eventually make the Warsaw exchange more attractive to foreign investors currently put off by its low market cap.
"Many foreigners worry about the weighting of Poland in international indices. If that weighting goes up...that will encourage more foreign investors," Korona's Skipper said.
But some analysts said the public offerings might have to be launched in the first half, before the parliamentary elections due in the late third quarter or fourth.
The governing leftist coalition will face populist rightist parties including the political wing of the Solidarity trade union.

Analysts said the election uncertainty could dampen demand but that its outcome might not significantly change economic policy, even if populist parties hitherto critical of economic reform and privatisation came out on top.

"Privatisation means certain money for the government -- you can't on the one hand promise people more money and on the other hand slow privatisations which are a serious source for the budget," said Remigiusz Tarka, of IB Austria Securities.
Analysts also said the planned first-half listing of National Investment Funds (NFIs) in Poland's mass privatisation scheme would widen the bourse's offer an attract more players.
They said an earnings rebound could be in store for some firms in the first quarter after this year's harsh weather.

Analysts also said an improvement in the German business cycle was counted on to boost Polish industry, though Taylor noted that the German rebound had already been pushed back and might not materialise until the third quarter.
Some analysts said 1997 could be the year for small-cap stocks to shine.

"Probably some of the smaller-cap stocks will be better performers just because the big-cap stocks have been the story of the year in 1996," said Merrill Lynch's Pettyfer, adding that small construction stocks could do well.
